newsitem.title: USA: UAW sets strike deadlines at GM parts plants.
newsitem.headline: UAW sets strike deadlines at GM parts plants.

text.p: The United Auto Workers said Tuesday it issued new strike deadlines at two GM plants in Michigan and Indiana, again threatening General Motors Corp. with parts shortages that could paralyse its operations.
The UAW said its members may walk off the job at midnight July 22 at a transmission plant in Warren, Mich., and a lighting and interior plant in Anderson, Ind., if no new contract is reached.

Union and GM negotiators have been trying for nearly three months to settle a costly walkout at the automaker's pickup truck plant in Pontiac, Mich. But UAW spokesman Reginald McGhee insisted there was no link between the new deadlines and the Pontiac strike.
"Any pressure that would occur to General Motors is the result of negotiations at these two plants," McGhee said. "If they reach agreement prior to the deadline, then those situations don't occur."

Analysts speculated last month that other strike deadlines at two parts plants in Michigan and one in Wisconsin were also meant to spur the Pontiac talks. Although the Pontiac strike remained unresolved, those contracts were settled without a walkout.

About 5,800 workers walked off the job April 22 at the Pontiac plant. The UAW says GM needs to add more jobs to ease overtime burdens. GM said it is trying to hold down costs as it prepares to introduce a new version of its C/K pickup truck that will require 30 percent fewer workers.
Talks at the Pontiac plant continue, UAW officials said Tuesday.
GM, which reports its second-quarter earnings Wednesday, has said the Pontiac strike and a second walkout at its Oklahoma City car plant have cost it $490 million in profits.

Both of the deadlines issued Tuesday are at plants that make critical components for GM. The Warren plant supplies four-speed automatic transmissions for cars and light trucks, including GM's new minivans. About 3,000 people work at the plant, said Al Benchich, president of Local 909 in Warren.
Benchich said contract talks have stalled over staffing and outsourcing, the practice of farming out work to outside suppliers.
"The issues are basically the same issues throughout all of General Motors," he said. "Not enough people and outsourcing of jobs."
About 2,500 workers at UAW Local 663 in Anderson make tail lamps and brake lights for nearly all GM vehicles, said GM spokeswoman Sharon Morton. She declined to comment on the strike deadline.
